utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know. I don't remember. It was a long time ago. But someone must have told me to work this way or another, because there are many people higher up from me in the hierarchy. I'm at the very bottom, and I can only obey orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further re-exam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your testimony is completed, and we thank you for travelling to assist the Tribunal. You're now released, and we wish you a safe passage back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready with its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours may recall -- I'm sorry, in court as you may have noticed. We don't have another witness. It would have been Ms. Hanson, if it hadn't been for everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, may I -- may I -- I did mention to your legal officer that because I anticipated this might happen, that it might be an opportunity to deal with the matter of the admission of documents which has been causing some problems, obviously, throughout the trial so far. It's a matter of, Your Honours, whether you're prepared to hear me on this day. I've alerted both my friends for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what seems to be happening at the moment is that Your Honours are, first of all, saying what is the relevance of the documents. We understand that, and I think we've discussed how we deal with that. That's one thing. But we seem to be moving further to a rather strict policy that applies to whether the document comes in through a witness. Namely, either the witness must be able to recognise the signature or in some way give a great deal of corroborative evidence about the contents of the document or in some other way be able to prove the authenticity of the document. Now, Your Honours' guideline on this, if I can just find it again, which was guideline 4: "There is no rule which prohibits the admission into evidence of documents merely because their alleged source was not called to testify. Likewise, the fact that a document has neither a signature nor a stamp is not in its reason -- in itself a reason to find that the document is not authentic." Your Honours, what has been happening for the last few days in particular is that we've asked -- let's take this last document, the list of policemen from Brcko. The witness yesterday was asked about that document and was able to identify the people that he said were involved in this ill-treatment from that list. It is clearly a vital document of relevance because who is or who is not a police officer is one of the major issues in this case and has been all along. So if there's a list that shows that these men are the police officers who were working at Brcko at the relevant period, then we would submit that it should be admitted as an exhibit, because the witness is able to say, "Though I didn't draw up the document, these names are the names I recognise." We have the same -- with the same document this morning, it's still not been admitted as an exhibit. Now, Your Honour, the problem is this: We didn't cater for a strict rule of admissibility, in other words, that there must be ability to recognise the signature or the contents, we'll talk about the contents of the documents. If we have to do that, then we will obviously be increasing -- we will have to increase the number of witnesses which we tried to reduce. Our submission is -- and I'm surprised that the Defence are taking these what I would suggest are technical objections, because they may find that it's what's sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, but when they try to present documents we object if those strict rules aren't there. We would suggest that the policies that are set out by 89(C), once we've established it's relevant, then the document should be admitted -- I'll just turn up 89. (C) -- well, first of all, "A Chamber shall apply -- 89 (A), a Chamber shall apply the rules of evidence set forth in this section and shall not be bound by national rules of evidence," which Judge Harhoff has already pointed out to us. "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." Your Honours, there are a number of decisions, I've brought them with me, and I can cite them. Perhaps -- there's only one Appeals Chamber decision on it and that was in the case of Galic, which was a long time ago, 7th of June, 2002 that were in effect they just say -- it deals mainly with hearsay evidence. Trial Chambers have a broad discretion under Rule 89(C) to admit relevant hearsay evidence. So it's really hearsay evidence, but all the rules say the test is relevance and probative value. And we would submit, for example, that while there was a document the other day which was a letter addressed to the minister of the interior, that is relevant in this case because what the defendant Mico Stanisic was informed about or his ministry was informed about is relevant, it may not be signed or sealed, and that, we would submit, merely attaches to the weight that Your Honours give to it rather and than its admissibility as a document. So effectively, what's happening at the moment is we ask for it to be admitted, the Defence object, perhaps the best result we get is marked for identification, which is actually just stacking up a huge number of documents. And if we simply put in all the documents through a bar-table motion, then Your Honours won't have any witness evidence on it, and we will simply set out why we say it's relevant and it will all, depending on Your Honours' decision, of course, because it's your discretion, come in without witnesses being asked about it. So, Your Honours, what we're suggesting is that the test should be not as particularly Mr. Cvijetic has been suggesting each time whether the signature can be recognised or whether it's got a seal or a stamp, but simply, is this a document about which the witness can speak either as to its contents or as to its relevance. And so that's -- those are our submissions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your -- Your Honours, very short submission. First of all, the position of the Defence is not what -- what my learned friend has just explained. The problem that we have, and I think the Trial Chamber shared our view in that respect, is the nexus between the particular witness and the document. The point of the matter that is if the -- if -- the witness today, he was shown a military document he doesn't know anything about, and then this document was -- because this military document talks about some events that happened, this witness was asked that this document be admitted. I really couldn't find any nexus, and that is the gist of our -- most of our objections. The same thing goes with the witness before. He was shown -- he was a victim who was kept in the -- in a detention centre, yes, and now he's shown a document with the list -- with the -- so the formal document, a list of whatever it is of the -- of the MUP members of Brcko or somewhere in September 1992. There is completely no nexus between him and that document. And that is -- that is the gist of our -- of our objections in all these cases. Now, I understand the problems that the -- that our friends are facing, but that is -- that is precisely why there is jurisprudence in this Tribunal that there are bar-table motions. So all the documents where they could not find or need not find a witness who will have enough nexus with the document they offer it on the bar table. They give an explanation why, the authenticity and all that, we respond, and that is it. And they can -- after that they can rely on that document in their final submissions. I mean, that is, as far as I know, the jurisprudence so far in this Tribunal. So what I'm trying to say is that we are -- we don't have to invent the hot water. We have the situation which is -- which is already adopted in this Tribunal, and I don't see why we should modify that, because I honestly think that it doesn't help either the Prosecutor or the Defence or Your Honours to have -- to have a document produced during the testimony of the witness where there is completely no nexus between that particular document and that witness. That is -- that is our submission. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And while we are on the same topic, for the record, the Zupljanin Defence is absolutely in support of the submission of our colleague Mr. Zecevic. The main issue from our point of view is the nexus. You as well-experienced fact-finders will certainly find the basis in each particular case, because we cannot have an overall approach with this regard. And let me respectfully remind you about the words and submission of Honourable Judge Harhoff with regard to the situation with previous witness, Mr. Delic, who was a prosecutor. And when we are dealing with a bundle of documents among which many of them were signed by particular witness, and in terms of judicial economy, in terms of avoiding overloading, sort of say, of -- of case with enormous number of exhibits, I think that you will find proper and right ruling in this particular situation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just in response say this: Of course we agree there has to be some nexus. We can't just show any old document that has no nexus to the witness. But for example, let's take the example of where the -- that the witness yesterday said, here is this list of police officers. I can say that the people who told me what police officers had these names and here's a list. I cannot think of a closer nexus quite honestly. And equally one has a military document that described an event that the witness can talk about from his own personal knowledge and then he says, "And this -- although, of course, I personally have never seen this document, but this is a military document from," let us say, "the 1st Krajina Corps --" I can see Mr. Zecevic shaking his head, but can I finish and then I'll -- that he -- the document itself shouldn't have that nexus with the witness because they're talking about the same event.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just very briefly. But the whole point in my submission was that this witness cannot confirm that this is the document of the 1st Krajina Corps. He can't. It is very -- as Mr. Cvijetic said, it was very simple. He should have given his recollection, like he did, his recollection of the events of -- at a certain point in time in Brcko because he was there. Now, my learned friend can use this document and help -- help him recollect his memory by stating, "Do you remember this? Do you remember this?" I mean, that would -- the result is basically the same. The problem is exactly that one: There is no nexus between him and that document. That is my opinion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If I may respond to some of the documents that have been made. I would like to begin by recalling that during the pre-trial stage of this trial, I as the Pre-Trial Judge made no secret of pointing out that the Trial Chamber, once we got to trial, would seek to be restrictive in its admission of evidence, because experience from all other trials before this Tribunal is that the amount of evidence that comes before the Judges is just so overwhelming and in the end, much of the evidence that is brought before us has limited relevance and limited probative value in relation to the charges that are raised in the indictment. So I think that there is a legitimate interest on the part of all the Chambers to try and really seek to limit the evidence that comes in to what is strictly necessary to prove the points that are raised in the indictments. Having said this, obviously the test for admission is a three-prong test. It has to be relevant, it has to have probative value, and there has to be some sort of nexus between the witness and the document. Now, obviously it is the nexus prong that has caused some uncertainty here in the last few days. Neither of the parties today have raised the difficulty that the Chamber has experienced, and that is this: What do we do if a witness is confronted with a document and the document says something and the witness says something completely different? So if there is a clear inconsistency between the information included in the document and the evidence provided by the witness. That's the difficulty we had with the two documents that we MFI'd today. The only thing that I can say on behalf of the Chamber is that these cases will have to be taken on a case-by-case basis, because it is very difficult to establish a general rule to these things, to this sort of problem. And obviously if the Chamber were to say that the witness must not only be able to comment on the events described in the documents but must also be able to confirm the truthfulness and the accuracy of the information contained in the document, if we were to say that this is a criterion for admission, then I think we would certainly be able to achieve the goal of restricting the -- the evidence, but that might also be to go too far. If, on the other hand, the Chamber were to say, well, as long as the witness can just comment on the information contained in the document, that is enough for admissibility, I think that would be perhaps to -- to be too lenient. So the Chamber is trying on a case-by-case basis to steer through somewhere in the middle of these two extreme points. The best thing I can suggest is that the parties, when you bring evidence to the Court, that you yourself take into consideration whether this document can and indeed should be admitted through this witness, or maybe whether you would wish to perhaps have another go with it with another witness who is more likely to confirm that what is contained in the document is actually authentic and correct. Now, as for the document yesterday, as I recall, Mr. Gashi was put -- was confronted with a list of policemen, and it was the Prosecution's submission that the next witness would be someone who could actually confirm, and I think the natural thing to do in that situation was to do exactly what the Chamber did, and they need to say, well, if there is a witness who himself was a policeman and whose name appears on the list, then it just felt more natural to have that document introduced through that next witness rather than through Mr. Gashi. So these are at least my personal observations. I don't know if my brothers have anything to add, but I think to repeat my personal suggestion to the parties is that try yourself to -- to take into consideration whether all the documents that you bring before us need to come into evidence, and if they do, then for what purpose, and consider if they should perhaps be introduced through another witness, in particular in cases where the witness clearly denies or says, "I have no knowledge about what the document pertains to -- to include." That's where the Chamber sees a difficulty. Now what are we supposed to do with this document that is clearly contradicted by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that -- can I say straightaway, I fully accept that there's no point in showing a document which says, "I don't know anything about it and I don't remember it happening like that." That's foolish. What I was concerned about, if you like, are the halfway house documents. You know, where the witness can't say that he's never seen it before but can say I recognise these names and, yes, they were there, and these events happened as this document reflects. Now, Your Honour, of course the bar-table motion which, Mr. Zecevic is very keen on, is of course a way of dealing with it and we can do the whole -- every document on our list, but it seems to me that's not right either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just add to what I said a few comments about the bar-table issue. Since we are not operating by a system that is truly adversarial nor in a system that is truly inquisitorial but somewhere in between, the issue of a dossier does not arise really, but the method of admitting documents through the bar table has been developed here as a means to somehow compensate for the attempts made by most Chambers to try and limit the evidence, and I think the bar-table option is and should remain an exception where a few documents in the end that perhaps a party forgot to have admitted or for some other reason was not admitted while there was a chance to do so can then be admitted through the bar table. But I would not like to see that we have in the end a huge load of documents that all need to be introduced through the bar table. The bar table should remain a very limited option.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, can I just say, there's one problem, and that's a problem -- a matter I've been discussing is the witness particularly who is coming on Tuesday, in theory can deal with a massive number of documents, all signed by him or part of government programmes. Now -- but if he has to deal with them all, the three hours that I'm going to be asking for for him is going to be doubled, and so I was hoping to deal with the most important ones, because in his testimony before the Krajisnik Chamber, which I think Your Honour will be familiar with, it was pretty short and only a few documents were dealt with, whereas obviously -- and all these documents are on our 65 ter list. There are many documents that he can deal with, if he so chooses, which is another matter. So if Your Honours are of the view that if a witness can deal with a document it should be put to him, then I think it's going to take a little bit longer. Whereas we were hoping to put some, for example, Assembly minutes simply in as bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. It depends on the nature of the documents a bit. Again, I stress the case-by-case approach that the Chamber is taking. If you're speaking about a whole batch of documents that are virtually of the same nature, same kind, my suggestion would be to deal with a few of the most important of those and seek to have them admitted, and then the question arises whether it would really be necessary to have all the others admitted into evidence as well. I mean -- what can I think of? If the issue, for instance, just as an example, is that you wish to show how reports were made from a SJB to the CSB and then you wish to show your point by presenting a hundred such reports, then I think -- I don't know if the Defence wishes to take issue with it, but the issue would then be that -- that either the Chamber will accept through the admission of a few of those documents that this was a routinely done thing and the witness that you bring can then confirm that "This is how we did it," and then if the Defence is ready to accept that this was the procedure, then I don't see the need to have all the hundred reports admitted into evidence. Then we will take the witness's word for it, and so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm trying to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. Your Honour will recall that in fact we raised that very matter and we produced a chart which Your Honour has some difficulty in grasping not surprisingly but the second matter is, for example, can I take Assembly minutes, the Bosnian Serb Assembly minutes. I was proposing to ask Tuesday's witness about a couple of them but each and every one of them contains matters which are relevant in particular to joint criminal enterprise, so we were hoping to deal with this witness, possibly one other, somewhere he spoke himself, but then put them all in under the bar-table motion as a bulk exhibit. I don't think it is possible to say there is one single Bosnian Serb Assembly minute which is not relevant in some way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be heard on a couple of matters. The first thing I will -- I will -- I will go back to page 58, 2 to 7, where my learned friend was talking about the halfway house documents. Your Honours, that is precisely the point. The document shown to the witness, perhaps in its first paragraph, talks about the certain event that the witness can remember, and he says, "Yes, that --" but the rest of the document he doesn't know anything about. There might -- this document might contain some issues which are very important, some other issues which are very important. Now, in case you would admit that document, then we would need to cross-examine the witness through that particular -- then we would need to cross-examine the witness and ask him paragraph by paragraph, do you remember this, do you know this, do you know this, do you know this, do you know this, do you know this, in order to find out at the very end that except this, this little piece of the document, he knows nothing else about. That is the problem that we are having. When the document is introduced only by -- let's say there is a letterhead, it says ministry of what, and you show it to the witness, do you know that the ministry existed, he says, yes, can we have the document admitted. That is what I'm talking about. That is my concern. The second thing, with all due respect, Your Honours, the issue of the communications is the issue that we intend to challenge. The number means nothing. Let me explain you. The normal -- in a normal situation, the ministry, from this -- in a case where it has six CSBs and a number of SJBs, let's say 50, the ministry should receive at least a thousand -- thousand communications per day. That is the -- the average what each and every minister of interior in all the countries of the world receives. Now, if the -- if the Prosecutor shows there is a hundred over four or six months, then of course it is not -- there is a problem in there. There has to be some problem, and there has to be some explanation. Now that is the issue, and that is why each and every of these documents have to be explained or this issue needs to be addressed by the parties. That is -- that is the number two. Number three: Your Honours, I have a problem with the -- with the minutes of the -- of the -- of the Assembly. Your Honours, the Assembly is a democratic thing. You have people who are the representatives of the -- of the -- of their particular community. They come in. They say their mind. This has nothing -- I mean, in my honest opinion, this has nothing to do -- this cannot be a basis for joint criminal enterprise. Not at all. This is -- we have the forum where people can say whatever they mean. They might have -- they might challenge this or challenge that, vote for that, not -- vote no for the other thing. I don't really see the relevance of that. I would -- I would understand that the certain portions of these transcripts are like an illustration presented to -- to the Trial Chamber and out of that the Prosecution builds their case, but that is exactly what they are doing through -- through the -- through the alleged experts that they want to -- that we are taking issue with. Now, that is why I think it is -- it is in fact doubling, because all this -- all what is important is what the experts are going to talk about, and now we want to introduce the whole documentation, and it's -- it's minutes of the -- of the forum, of the most democratic forum that the civilisation knows. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels, I'm sure you can recall that during the pre-trial phrase when we had the 65 ter meetings a great number of times the Pre-Trial Judge invited the parties, the Defence and Prosecution, to identify the issues that were contested and that needed to be proven at trial, and most often the Pre-Trial Judge was told off because he was told, "Ah, we're not going to discuss this at this stage. That will be evident at trial." Now we are at trial, and -- and so now is the time when the parties have to show their hand. So if there is an issue about -- I'm just mentioning as an example if there is an issue about how the communication lines went from the SJB to the CSB to the MUP, then those issues have to be clarified, and the Prosecution will bring evidence to show how it worked, and the Defence may bring evidence to challenge the point that the Prosecution is trying to make and say that it doesn't -- it didn't function the way the Prosecution tells us it did, but it functioned in some other way, or it didn't function at all. And -- and so my comment is to return to the invitation that was made to the parties during the pre-trial phase to actually try and identify the issues that are -- that are contested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know why the parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's my turn --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. We said over and over again that the Defence pre-trial briefs were utterly defective, we were not being told what the issues were, and Your Honour tried to make them declare what the issues were as you say got told off, but not us, we have said over and over again these issues should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just point to the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... is defective. That's -- please do not misinterpret our position. One minute, Your Honour. One minute, please. Thanks God we are in the hand of professional Judges. With all due respect. I have great respect for all Judges within this Tribunal, but some of them being a diplomat or professors or academic might not be focused for the core of the case, and I will tell you simply what is the position of Zupljanin Defence. Point number one, Your Honours, we are wasting enormous amount of time here with history, politics, I don't know which kind of assumptions, due to the broad and groundless theory of joint criminal enterprise pushed by this Prosecution without any particular basis in illegal system. That's why we have to -- that's why we have to waste time with Assembly meetings and stuff like that. If you can direct Prosecution to drop charges for -- for this extremely broad third category of JCE, which means nothing, then we could have more efficient trial. Otherwise, Defence is obliged to response to enormous ocean, space of various documents and then we are wasting time here, Your Honour. Case is very simple. If they have proofs that my client ordered, instigated, or committed certain crimes, okay. Give me the evidence. What does it mean Assembly or Crisis Staff or history of here and there? Thank you so much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm afraid that once again we have abused the services of the interpreters. We are far over the time where we should have had a break, and I suggest we take the break now, at least, and if there is a need to continue this discussion, then we can meet after 20 minutes, but if not, then I suggest we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I have all time of my life. I can -- I can discuss this matter, you know, days and days if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know there's much point. I think we've raised the real issue, and I see Mr. Zecevic nodding, who doesn't perhaps quite take the extreme views expressed by Mr. Pantelic, but we actually were going to use the time today to try and finally decide on the laws so that we could put the package in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So we adjourn now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we adjourn now, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are in Courtroom II on when we resume on Monday morning at 9.00. Thank you. I trust everyone has a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And thank you to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.
